faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Saluda attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: South Carolina law does not work that way. SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and an animal captured near a home must be destroyed or, only with a separate department permit, may be relocated. In Saluda we solve it with eviction and exclusion instead: a one-way door lets the raccoon leave the attic on its own, or the animal is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then every entry around farm-town center and Mine Creek neighborhoods of the county seat housing is sealed in steel. Raccoons are the top rabies carrier in SC Department of Public Health testing, so droppings and latrine areas are cleaned and sanitized as part of the job.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Saluda home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes we are called about in Saluda are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs around farm-town center and Mine Creek neighborhoods of the county seat. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide and the venomous snake we encounter most in the Upstate and Midlands. Identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, note where it went, and call us. Venomous snakes are safety-and-identification work, not a guaranteed capture, and the lasting fix is usually habitat — clearing brush, woodpiles, and rodent shelter near the house.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Saluda actually involve?
faqs.a: It starts with the inspection, and the scope grows or shrinks with what that inspection finds around farm-town center and Mine Creek neighborhoods of the county seat: how many entry points the animal has opened, whether young are present, and how much exclusion the roofline and crawlspace need. A single squirrel entry sealed in a day is a small job; a raccoon family with latrine cleanup and a full roofline seal is a larger one. We walk you through each item we find before the work is set, so the scope you approve is the scope we do.

Saluda.wildlife_intro:
In Saluda, most of our work starts around the farm-town center and Mine Creek neighborhoods of the county seat. More than anything else, we are called for raccoons in brick-ranch attics and gray squirrels chewing into soffits.

Brick ranches from the 1960s and 1970s, older in-town homes near the center, and fast-growing subdivisions at the edges give this housing stock three distinct generations of rooflines to inspect. River and lake country surrounds these neighborhoods — creeks, coves, and wooded drains run behind the subdivisions — giving raccoons, squirrels, and bats a covered route to almost every roofline.

The last step on a Saluda call is a walk-around with the homeowner: each entry we sealed, each burrow we screened, and what to watch for when the seasons turn.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Ward home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: How do rats get into Monetta homes?
faqs.a: Around Monetta, rats follow food and cover: bird feeders, pet food, ivy and brush against the house, and the lines and limbs that reach the roof near farm country toward the Aiken line in the county's south. The job is trapping inside, sealing every entry we find, and cutting the routes and food that drew them. We will show you the droppings and rub marks we used to confirm the species, because rat work fails when it is guessed at.

faqs.q: How does bat removal work in Monetta?
faqs.a: In Monetta, bat work means exclusion only: one-way devices on the main entries, every other opening sealed, and the colony leaves on its own at dusk. South Carolina does not require a permit for bat removal, and we time full exclusions to SCDNR's guidance windows — early spring or August through October — to avoid trapping flightless young during the summer maternity season. Guano cleanup follows once the attic is empty.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my Monetta house?
faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a Monetta job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near farm country toward the Aiken line in the county's south with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.

faqs.q: Why do skunks keep denning under Monetta homes and outbuildings?
faqs.a: Southwestern Saluda County gives skunks everything they want in one short walk: pasture grubs and fallen feed, brushy creek bottoms for cover, and quiet, dark voids under the skirting of manufactured homes and the floors of barns and feed rooms. In late winter a female picks exactly that kind of sheltered space to raise a litter, and the smell usually arrives before the first sighting. Our crew checks every raised foundation on the property, removes the animals under South Carolina's depredation-permit rules, and then closes the skirting and floor gaps with buried wire so the next skunk cannot simply move into the same void.

Monetta.wildlife_intro: Monetta sits in the far southwestern corner of Saluda County, a small farming crossroads where the paved streets give out quickly into pasture, pine woods and creek bottomland toward the Aiken County line. The calls that define this town are farm-edge calls: skunks denning under outbuildings, feed rooms and the skirting of manufactured homes, raccoons working sweet-corn patches and chicken runs, and gray squirrels moving between the mature pines that shade nearly every lot. Because most properties here run on acreage rather than subdivision lots, a Monetta job usually starts with a walk of the whole place — house, barn, well house and woodline — before a single trap is set. Animals travel the creek corridors from one farm to the next, so sealing one building without checking the outbuildings rarely holds. Our crew handles that full circuit in one visit and tells you plainly which structures are active and which are just available.
